                                         Figure 1. Overview of our Guideline-Driven Clustering Agent. We introduce the first universal clustering framework that handles
                                         diverse image clustering scenarios through textual guidelines, spanning from general to fine-grained tasks, from global to local criteria, and
                                         from balanced to long-tail distributions. Our training-free hybrid agent flexibly adapts across these diverse clustering requirements.

vious methods fail to achieve. GCPM captions augment                    verse clustering tasks. The first stage, Generative Con-

Figure 2. Overview of the Clustering Framework. Bottom left: Generative Concept Proxy Modeling extracts guideline-aware textual
descriptions from images via multimodal LLM and encodes them into embeddings for efficient clustering; Right: MST-based LLM Traver-
sal refines initial clusters by constructing a Minimum Spanning Tree and selectively querying the LLM for semantic merging decisions.
Top left: For scenarios without available guidelines, we introduce heuristic prompts for automatic guideline generation.

tual form, containing multiple criteria that users wish to                          images and guidelines using multimodal instruction-aware
consider for clustering. Formally, a guideline G contains                           embedding models [32, 48, 55, 93] introduces critical lim-

G, where A represents the universal set of possible at-                             sive clustering scenarios, fine-grained attributes mentioned
tributes. For instance, in bird species clustering [78], G                          in guidelines may be overshadowed if they are not explic-
might include attributes such as “tail shape” and “wing                             itly queried. Moreover, in dimension-specific clustering, ir-
color”. In scenarios where explicit guidelines are unavail-                         relevant but visually salient attributes can dominate the in-
able, we leverage the internal knowledge of LLMs [1] to                             tended attributes.
generate appropriate clustering guidelines. We introduce                                We address this through a concept proxy approach. We

3.3. MST-based LLM Traversal                                                Iterative Guideline-Driven LLM Merging Instead of
GCPM provides a training-free and efficient embedding ap-                   merging clusters recursively until all are combined, we it-
proach for clustering. For scenarios where cluster num-                     eratively query an LLM to decide whether pairs of clusters
bers are predetermined, K-Means can be directly applied.                    should be merged. In each iteration, after computing the
However, in many real-world tasks, clusters are automat-                    distance matrix and MST, we present cluster pairs to the
ically discovered following guideline specifications rather                 merging LLM [3] fmerge in order of increasing distance:
than predefined knowledge. An intuitive solution is to apply
                                                                              p = fmerge (G, Ci , Cj ), for each edge (Ci , Cj ) ∈ T. (8)
algorithms that do not require predefined cluster numbers,
such as HDBSCAN [6], to guideline-aware embeddings.                         The LLM evaluates a cluster pair based on the provided
                     C = HDBSCAN(H).                             (5)        guideline G and generates a binary decision p ∈ {0, 1}
                                                                            whether they should be merged. Each cluster is represented
In practice, we observe that HDBSCAN tends to generate                      by GCPM captions of Top-K (K=5) samples nearest to the
consistent small clusters but fails to merge homogeneous                    centroid. The process continues until either all appropriate
clusters into larger groups. It indicates that HDBSCAN ef-                  clusters are merged or the LLM decides no further merg-
fectively groups clearly similar samples together. But for                  ing is beneficial. To further improve efficiency, we cache
scenarios involving larger sample volumes or more com-                      LLM decisions from previous iterations to avoid redundant
plex sample variations, it is less effective due to the density-            queries for previously evaluated pairs. We discuss its effi-
based nature. To address this limitation, we propose using                  ciency improvement in the Appendix A.2.

    In contrast, K-Means produces comparable precision and
recall. This balanced performance can be attributed to the
prior knowledge of cluster numbers, which forces the algo-
rithm to aggregate more samples into larger groups. After
applying MST Traversal, we observe a substantial improve-
ment in Recall with only a modest sacrifice in Precision. It
demonstrates that the LLM successfully merges most small
clusters into larger, semantically coherent groups accord-           Figure 5. Comparison of LLM calls used for clustering and their

merge rate model assumption that the LLM merges clusters
more frequently at the beginning, and the merge probabil-                  Figure 7. Raw sample examples from the original ABO dataset.
ities decrease as clusters become more refined. Notably,
if the LLM rejects a pair, they will exist in the next iter-
ation and may be selected again by the MST. As merging                    the ABO-LC dataset does not have an explicit definition for
becomes less frequent in later iterations, more and more                  each category, reflecting real-world scenarios and making
rejected pairs will be repeatedly selected. Therefore, we                 the clustering process even more challenging.
cache decisions for all rejected pairs and skip them if they
occur subsequently. This cache mechanism reduces the                      B.2. Existing Datasets and Metrics

                                                                    5
I want to cluster a dataset of dog images based on dog breeds.

What are the major differences I should consider when distinguishing between different dog
breeds?
Please list the key categories of differences that would help identify and separate different
breeds.

Keep your answer concise and structured.

When distinguishing dog breeds, consider these major categories:

1. Size and body structure

2. Head and facial features

3. Coat characteristics

4. Body proportions and limb structure

5. Distinctive breed-specific traits

Based on the major difference categories for dog breeds:
1. Size and body structure
2. Head and facial features
3. Coat characteristics
4. Body proportions and limb structure
5. Distinctive breed-specific traits

Please identify the specific visual attributes within each category that can be observed in dog
images. For each attribute, provide examples of variations (e.g., for size: small, medium, large,
giant). Format your response as a structured list of attributes with their possible values.


Visual Attributes for Dog Breed Clustering:

SIZE AND BODY STRUCTURE:
- Size: small (e.g., Chihuahua), medium (e.g., Border Collie), large (e.g., German Shepherd),
giant (e.g., Great Dane)
- Body proportions: square vs. rectangular builds, leggy vs. low-to-ground
- Musculature: athletic/lean vs. stocky/robust

HEAD AND FACIAL FEATURES:
- Skull shape: brachycephalic (flat-faced like Bulldogs), mesocephalic (medium like
Labradors), dolichocephalic (long-nosed like Collies)
- Ear type: erect (German Shepherd), semi-erect (Siberian Husky), rose (Greyhound), button
(Fox Terrier), dropped (Basset Hound)
- Muzzle length: short to long
- Facial features: wrinkles, jowls, distinctive markings

COAT CHARACTERISTICS:
- Length: short (Beagle), medium (Golden Retriever), long (Afghan Hound)
- Texture: smooth, wire, curly, wavy, corded
- Color patterns: solid, bicolor, tricolor, brindle, merle, spotted, ticked
- Density: single coat vs. double coat

LIMBS AND TAIL:
- Tail: curled (Spitz breeds), straight, docked, bushy
- Leg length: short to long

C.2. Detailed Guideline
                                                                    Multiple-clustering with user-specified aspects. Recent
As mentioned in Section 3.1, we consider a guideline G that
                                                                    works such as Multi-MaP [90] and Multi-Sub [89] focus on
contains multiple attributes A = {a1 , a2 , · · · , ak } ⊆ G.
                                                                    multiple clustering, where a dataset can be partitioned from
Table 15 shows all attributes considered for each dataset.
                                                                    different perspectives, for example ”by color” versus ”by
Based on these attributes, three types of guideline prompts
                                                                    species” for fruits. They typically construct proxy spaces or
are derived: the GCPM captioning prompts (shown in Ta-
                                                                    subspaces aligned with user-specified aspects, often using
bles 16, 17, 18, 19) generate GCPM captions based on all at-
                                                                    CLIP plus a small number of aspect words as anchors, and
tributes; the instruction-aware embedding prompts (shown
                                                                    then train an end-to-end deep clustering model to produce
in Table 20) encode the GCPM captions based on one at-
                                                                    aspect-specific partitions. While they support user-specified
tribute or a global definition of all attributes; and the MST
                                                                    criteria, they (1) require dataset-specific training or fine-
Traversal prompts (some shown in Table 21 due to space
                                                                    tuning, (2) mainly target balanced and relatively small-scale
constraints) consider one attribute or a global definition of
                                                                    benchmarks such as Fruit, Cards, and CIFAR10-MC, and
all attributes for merging a pair of clusters.
                                                                    (3) still assume a small number of discrete aspect choices

We leverage three embedders: Instructor-large [72], E5-             Clustering with External Guidance (TAC) [45] introduces

ments. In general, they can be classified into two cate-            Net concepts into the representation space. TAC first builds

modal instruction-aware embedders, as shown in Figure 8.            via CLIP, and then jointly distills image and text cluster
For Instructor-large and E5-Mistral, the input consists of          heads with a mutual-distillation objective. This improves
the GCPM caption and the instruction-aware embedding                general image clustering without labels, but the ”guidance”
prompt. For GME-QWen, the input consists of the orig-               is limited to a fixed concept vocabulary and cannot express
inal image, the GCPM caption, and the instruction-aware             complex multi-attribute business rules or fine-grained op-
embedding prompt.                                                   erational guidelines. The method is also tied to a specific

                                      Table 10. Comparison of key guideline-aware and LLM/VLM-driven clustering methods.

Paper                                 Task                                       Guideline Mechanism                         LLM/VLM Role                                      Limitation/Difference

Agentic Graph Traversal (Arxiv 2025) Personalized multiple clustering            User preferences bias graph & traversal     MLLM agents expand/merge clusters                 High LLM cost; scaling issues
Multi-Sub (NeurIPS 2024)              Multi-view clustering with user criteria   GPT-4 proxy words (e.g., red, green)        Aligns images to subspaces                        Oversimplifies complex guidelines
IC|TC (ICLR 2024)                     Image clustering under user text criteria User text refined into cluster names         GPT-4 generates cluster names & assignments       Relies on text descriptions; limited fine-grained control
LiSA (ACL 2025)                       Topic modeling                             LLM generates candidate topics              Guides document–topic alignment                   Text-only; not visual
ClusterLLM (EMNLP 2023)               Text clustering                            Triplet/pairwise queries under instruction LLM judges similarity & granularity                Expensive; not image-focused
TAC (ICML 2024)                       Image clustering + external ontology       WordNet nouns as guidance                   CLIP + noun anchors                               Requires fixed ontology; not user-adaptive
TGAICC (Arxiv 2024)                   Multiple valid clusterings                 Different prompts → consensus               LLM generates criteria & consensus                Limited efficiency; unstable across prompts
ITGC (Arxiv 2025)                     Text-guided image clustering               Extracts and cluster in concept space       LLM produces concept-aligned embedding space      High-quality text needed; weak for fine-grained/hierarchy
X-Cluster/TeDeSC (Arxiv 2024)         Open-ended clustering                      Auto-discovers natural-language criteria    VLM + LLM propose grouping dimensions             Lack of control; exploratory, not precise
TGIC (EACL 2024)                      Caption-driven clustering                  Captions serve as criteria                  Text model augments embeddings                    Early/simple; weak guideline following
CLIP-Cluster (ICCV 2023)              Attribute-driven face clustering           Hallucinated CLIP attributes                CLIP acts as proxy feature extractor              Not LLM; limited to predefined attributes

ABO-LC “Item Name: item name
       Describe the e-commerce product based on its image and item name with a specific focus on required
       criteria.
       You should strictly follow the output format below:
       OUTPUT FORMAT: - Description: Provide a general description of the product here. - Brand: Provide
       the brand of the e-commerce product here, which might be inferred from the item name. - Model
       Name: Provide the model name of the e-commerce product here, which might be inferred from the
       item name. - Product Type: Provide the product type of the e-commerce product here, which might be
       inferred from the item name. - Style: Provide the style of the e-commerce product here, which might
       be inferred from the item name.”




                          Table 20. Instruction-Aware Embedding Prompts for Each Dataset.

Dataset          Instruction-Aware Embedding Prompt
CIFAR-10         Identify the object type based on the image description considering its physical characteristics,
                 habitat, and functional properties.
STL-10           Identify the category of the object based on the image description focusing on distinctive visual
                 and functional characteristics.
ImageNet-10      Identify the specific object category based on the image description considering its physical char-
                 acteristics, function, and distinctive features.
Fruit            Identify the species of the fruit based on the image description.
                 Identify the color of the fruit based on the image description.
Cards            Identify the number of the card based on the image description.
                 Identify the suit of the card based on the image description.
CIFAR10-MC       Identify the type of the object based on the image description.
                 Identify the environment where the object is based on the image description.
CUB Birds        Identify the species of the bird based on the image description.
Stanford Cars    Identify the type of the car based on the image description.
Stanford Dogs    Identify the breed of the dog based on the image description.
Oxford Flowers Identify the category of the flower based on the image description.
ABO-LC           Identify the variation of the product based on the description focusing on its brand, model name,
                 product type, and style




                                                        16
      Table 21. LLM Merging Prompts Used in MST Traversal for Cards conditioned on Number and Stanford Cars.

Dataset         LLM Merging Prompt in MST
Cards-Number “You are an agent for poker card image clustering. Your task is to determine whether two clusters
             of poker card images should be merged based on their representative images or image descrip-
             tions.
             (merge rules) 1. Please observe the main value of the cards for each cluster. If two clusters
             have the same value of cards, they should be merged. Otherwise, they should not be merged.
             (/merge rules)”

Stanford Cars   “You are an agent for car image clustering. Your task is to determine whether two clusters of car
                images should be merged based on their representative images or image descriptions.
                (merge rules) 1. Two clusters can be merged only if their images show cars with the same make,
                model, and year. Otherwise, they should not be merged. 2. ALL of the following features
                MUST match EXACTLY between clusters: - Make (manufacturer brand) - Model (specific car
                model name) - Year (production year) 3. ZERO TOLERANCE POLICY: - If ANY of these three
                features differ, DO NOT MERGE - Different years of the same make and model should NOT
                be merged - Different models from the same make should NOT be merged - Different trims or
                variants should be evaluated based on whether they are considered the same model 4. General
                appearance similarities are NOT sufficient for merging – the make, model, and year must match
                exactly. (/merge rules)”
